screens:
The session begins.

Morning comes to Beregost the way it always does here: first the bells of Lathander's temple, then the hammers. By the time the light slips through the shutters, half the town's forges are already ringing.

The room above the Lantern and Tongs is small and honest — a bed, a washstand, your gear where you left it, and the heavy purse that still feels like it belongs to someone luckier. Three hundred and fifty gold, give or take. No debt to collect, no caravan to guard, no one waiting for you anywhere today.

The cat is not on the bed. It sits by the door, tail curled around its paws, watching the gap under the frame with steady attention. A moment later you hear why, or part of why: heavy, unhurried steps on the stairs, and a woman's voice through the wood.

"Morning up there! Porridge and bacon's on, eggs if you're quick. Will you be wanting it brought up, or are you coming down?"

From the yard beneath the window drifts another sound — the clatter of a barrel being rolled into place, the slap of a deck being squared, and a carter calling out that there's room for one more if anyone's feeling lucky before the smith gets to their wheels.

The steps stop outside your door. The cat looks up at you.

Place: Rented room above the Lantern and Tongs, Beregost
Time: Day 1 · morning

The stairs of the Lantern and Tongs creak at every step. The common room below is warm and smells of fat and woodsmoke. Hedda Brask is already back behind the counter by the time you reach the bottom. She points you to a table near the hearth with the ladle in her hand, then disappears through the kitchen door. She comes back with a plate of three eggs, fried hard at the edges, bread, and a heap of bacon. She sets a saucer on the floor beside your boot. Two strips are cut small on it.

"For the gentleman with the ear," she says. Penny inspects the saucer as if checking it for poison, then eats with steady, unhurried dignity.

The room is half full. A dwarf in a scorched leather apron eats porridge alone with his back to the wall. He has a smith's forearms and doesn't look up. Two men in road-dusty coats share the table by the window. One is lean and anxious, the other heavy and calm, and they aren't keeping their voices down.

"…fourth one since Greengrass. Four wagons, Dalmer. Not robbed. *Gone*. Oxen, drivers, the lot."

"So you hire more guards."

"With what? The guards are the ones not coming back. And the Fist sends two riders as far as the Lion's Way and turns round. I asked."

The heavy one shrugs and tears his bread. "Then you go by the coast road."

"And add six days."

Through the open yard door, over the rhythm of the hammers, Orrin Tabb's voice rises cheerfully: "Nobody? Not one sporting soul in all Beregost? I'll deal you in for copper, friend, copper!" A deck snaps against the barrelhead. Nobody answers him.

A board by the door has a few papers nailed to it. One is new and still bright. From here you can make out the heavy lettering at the top: **GUARDS WANTED — NASHKEL ROAD — GOOD PAY**. There's smaller writing underneath that you'd have to get up to read.

Hedda comes back past your table with a jug and fills your cup without asking. She's wiping her hands on her apron.

"Breakfast's three silver with the cat's share. I'll put it on your reckoning or take it now, as you like." She glances at the window, where the anxious man has started counting on his fingers. "And will you be keeping the room another night, sir, or are you on the road today?"

James feels through the purse, and his fingers find nothing but gold. The Lady's winnings didn't come in small coin. He puts a single gold piece on the table instead. Hedda wipes her hands on her apron, picks it up, and counts seven silver back onto the wood without looking at them. She's done this ten thousand times.

"Five silver a night," she says. "That's the bed, a fire if you want one, and supper. Breakfast's extra, same as this morning. You can tell me by noon. After that I give it to whoever's knocking."

James glances at the window table. Hedda follows his look, and she points at it with the jug in her hand.

"That paper by the door is his. Master Lusk. He nailed it up last night and he's asked me twice since whether anyone's read it." She lowers the jug. "What he knows is his to tell. You'll have to ask him."

At the window, the lean man has stopped counting on his fingers. He has heard his name, though not what came with it. He looks across the room at James, then at the rapier, then at the cloak, the way a man prices a horse he can't afford. Dalmer keeps tearing his bread.

Penny has finished the bacon. She sits by the empty saucer and turns her head, the torn ear first, toward the window table.

Place: Common room of the Lantern and Tongs · Time: Day 1 · morning

Penny gets down from her place by the hearth and follows the plate across the room. She stays a pace behind James's boots, as if the bacon were still on it.

Dalmer looks up from his bread, looks at the plate, and pushes the salt cellar aside with one thick finger to make room. Lusk half rises, then sits again. He can't decide which would be more polite.

"Sit, please. Sit. Lusk. Hal Lusk. Cloth and salt, Beregost to Nashkel, ore and hides back." He talks fast, as if each sentence costs him something. "Nobody's come back, Master Worgen. That's the first thing. Not a driver, not an ox, not a wheel."

He leans in over the table.

"I've been robbed twice in twenty years. I know what it looks like. You find the wagon burnt in a ditch and the oxen butchered for meat. Somebody's always alive with his head broken, and he tells you how many there were. This time there's nothing. And the goods..." He taps the table. "Every bale I send has my mark on it, a blue L stitched in the corner. Bandits sell what they take, and they sell it close, because they can't carry it far. I've had men asking in Nashkel, here, at the Friendly Arm. Not one yard of my cloth has turned up. Nobody's salt has turned up. Four wagons, and nothing for sale anywhere."

"Tell him about Freely," Dalmer says, without looking up.

"I'm getting there." Lusk ticks the points off on his fingers. "The last one was Pell's wagon, eleven days ago. I paid a woodsman two gold to go and look, Tam Freely, he cuts timber south of town. About half a day past where the Fist riders turn round, he found where the ruts leave the road. They go east into the scrub, towards the hills. He followed them maybe a mile, to stony ground, and he lost them there. He wouldn't go any further. Said he'd been paid to look, not to follow."

Dalmer finally sets his bread down. "I drank with Freely after. He said there were no horses. Just the oxen, the wheels, and boots on both sides of the wagon. A lot of boots." He shrugs. "Make of it what you like."

James knows this part from his own years with the scouts, not from anyone's story. Iron tyres scrape stone. A loaded wagon leaves a trail across rocky ground too, if the man following knows to look for bright scratches instead of ruts. And men who take a wagon whole and drive it off the road on foot aren't after what's in it. In Tethyr he saw the free companies do the same thing to farmers' carts. They took the wagon, the beasts and the man holding the reins, because they had a baggage train to fill and somewhere to take it. That wasn't robbery. It was requisition.

Under the table, Penny has settled where she can watch Dalmer's boots and the door at once.

Lusk sees James's face and misreads it, or reads it right. He wets his lips. His eyes go to the old regimental cloak and stay on it.

"I've one wagon left. I'm sending it tomorrow at first light, because if I don't, I've nothing to sell in Nashkel this season, and then..." He stops before the sentence gets to money. "I need two blades. Three, if I can get them. A soldier and a scout... Are you looking for work, Master Worgen?"

· New place: Where Pell's wagon left the road
· Journal: “Wagons vanishing on the Nashkel road” updated
· New person: Tam Freely
· New person: Pell

Place: Common room of the Lantern and Tongs · Time: Day 1 · morning

Lusk looks at the fork, then at James. Something in his face eases a little, the way it does when a man hears his own fears said aloud by someone who isn't frightened of them.

"Magic," he says. He glances at Dalmer, who has stopped chewing. "Well. Well, that's... I won't say no to that."

He takes the questions in order, fast, like a man reading out a bill.

"Pay. Ten gold a head to Nashkel. Five now, five when the wagon's in the yard at Nashkel. Your board on the road is mine, and your bed in Nashkel the first night." He stops, wets his lips, and goes on before anyone can answer. "It's three days if the weather holds. That's better than the Fist pays a man for a month."

The figure comes out smoothly, too smoothly, like something he's said to himself in the dark a few times. The notice by the door said GOOD PAY. Ten gold is fair pay, not good pay.

"Who else. Nobody yet." He doesn't dress it up. "One fellow came by last night and read the paper. He asked where the wagons went missing and walked out. I'm driving it myself, if it comes to that. I've no drivers left to send."

Then his hands come up onto the table, and he counts without seeming to notice he's doing it.

"How many. First wagon, before Greengrass: Old Corran and his boy. Second: Wil Hask driving, two guards. Third: Bettany Marsh driving, two guards. Brothers, the guards were, from Nashkel. Fourth, Pell, with one guard. I couldn't afford two by then." His fingers stop. "Eleven. Eleven people. And Corran's boy was fourteen."

Dalmer sets down what's left of his bread. "Corran's wife comes here Tenday evenings to ask if there's word," he says to James, flatly. "In case you meet her."

Lusk stares at the table for a moment before going on.

"Freely. He's not here. Days he's at his cut south of town, down along the stream past the last forge. Follow the sound of the axe. Evenings he drinks at the Burning Wizard, across the square." He looks up. "I'll tell you now, he won't thank you for asking. He didn't like what he saw out there, and he liked it less once he'd been paid for it."

Dalmer grunts. "He'll talk to you. He won't go back."

Under the table, Penny has moved. She now sits by James's boot with her back to the room, so she can see Lusk's hands.

Lusk sees James's face and makes himself go on.

"You'd want to see him before you'd say yes. I understand that. I'd do the same." His voice drops. "But the wagon goes at first light, Master Worgen, with you or without you. I need to know by this afternoon, so I can find someone else if it's no."

· Time passes: 10 minutes
· New place: Burning Wizard
· New place: Tam Freely's timber cut
· Journal: “Wagons vanishing on the Nashkel road” updated
· New person: Corran's wife

Place: Common room of the Lantern and Tongs · Time: Day 1 · morning

Lusk nods too quickly, the way a man does when he has decided to hear "not yet" as better than "no."

"This afternoon. Yes. That's fair." He reaches for his cup, finds it empty and puts it down again. "Tell Freely I sent you. Or don't. He might talk more if you don't."

Dalmer says nothing. He pushes the last of the bread toward Penny, who looks at it and then at him, and does not take it.

You finish the eggs. The bacon has gone where bacon goes. Hedda is busy at the counter as you pass, and the board by the door gives you the small print on Lusk's notice at last: *Apply Hal Lusk, Lantern and Tongs. Wagon departs first light, 3rd inst.* Nothing more than that.

Outside, Beregost has fully woken. The main street is a long run of open forge doors, and each one breathes heat as you pass. A boy is leading two oxen to be shod. A Lathanderite acolyte in rose-coloured wool is chalking the price of candles on the temple wall. South of the square the houses thin out and the forges get rougher: lean-tos with stone hearths and slag heaps behind them. The last one is a dwarf-built shed with a black chimney. Past it the road drops to a stream, brown with run-off at the edges and clear in the middle, and a footpath follows it south into alder and ash.

The hammers fade behind you. Inside a quarter of an hour the loudest things are the water and Penny, who has decided the path is hers. She walks a few yards ahead with her tail up and stops now and then to look into the reeds as if they owed her money.

Then you hear the axe. The strokes come steady and unhurried, the sound of a man who swings for a living and doesn't waste any.

The cut is a clearing on the far bank, where the stream widens enough to wade. Trunks are stacked and barked along one side. A mule stands hobbled in the shade, and a two-wheeled timber cart has one shaft propped on a stump. In the middle of it all a man in his fifties is working an ash tree that is nearly down. He's wiry, grey-stubbled, and has his shirt off despite the morning chill. He sees you before you reach the water. The axe stops at the top of its swing, comes down slowly, and stays in his hand.

Penny halts on the near bank and sits. The mule's ears go flat at her.

The woodsman looks at the rapier, at the cloak, at the cat. When he speaks it's across the stream, flat, without raising his voice much.

"If Lusk sent you, I've had my two gold and I've told him what I saw. If he didn't, this is private timber." He shifts his grip on the haft. "Which is it?"

· Travel: Tam Freely's timber cut (35 minutes)

Place: Tam Freely's timber cut · Time: Day 1 · morning

Freely hears the name and lets out a short breath through his nose. It isn't quite a laugh. He doesn't put the axe down, but he lets the head rest on the ground and leans on the haft.

"Honest, anyway." He looks at you across the water for a while, then at Penny, who has started watching the mule. The mule watches her back. "Not asking me to go back. Good. I wouldn't."

He's quiet long enough that you start to think that's all you'll get. Then he jerks his chin south, toward the road.

"Past where the Fist riders turn round there's a dead oak, split by lightning, on the left side going south. Two hundred paces after that, east side. That's where it left the road. You'd not see it from the wagon seat. Somebody cut broom and swept the verge behind them, the first fifty feet or so. I only found it because they threw the broom in the ditch and it was wilting."

He shifts his grip on the haft.

"The boots. Dalmer told you a lot of boots. It's more than that. Nailed soles, same nails, same pattern, near enough every one. Two files of them, one each side of the wagon, keeping pace with the oxen. Nobody straggling and nobody stepping off to piss. I've tracked deer, and I've tracked lads poaching deer. Poachers wander. These didn't." He counts it in his head without moving his lips. "Ten. Twelve, maybe. Hard to tell, they walked in each other's prints."

You heard enough of this in Tethyr to fill in what he's left out. He's describing hobnailed marching boots, a column, and men on march discipline with a cart in the middle. It's the same picture you got at breakfast, and now somebody's actually seen it.

"Stony ground's about a mile in. Scrub gives out, it's all shelf rock and gravel, slopes up toward the hills. Trail stops there like a cut rope." He looks down at the axe head. "I stood there a while."

His thumb goes to the small leather pouch tied at his belt, rests on it for a moment, and comes away again. He doesn't look at it. He doesn't look at you either.

"Twelve men who march in step and sweep up after themselves don't want finding. Anyone who finds them ends up counted with the rest. That's why I turned round." He lifts the axe off the ground, not into a swing, just back into his hands. "That's what Lusk's two gold bought him. You can have it for nothing."

Then, flatly, his eyes back on you:

"You taking his wagon down there?"

· Time passes: 10 minutes

Place: Tam Freely's timber cut · Time: Day 1 · morning

Freely watches your eyes go to his belt and come back to his face. He doesn't hide the pouch, and he doesn't touch it again. The axe stays where it is, head down in the wood chips. On the near bank Penny has turned her torn ear toward him and gone still.

For a while the only sounds are the stream and the mule shifting its weight.

messages.text:
“Coming down. Eggs, please—and a little bacon for my stern companion.”

At the sound of the cards, my hand pauses over my purse. I tuck it firmly into my belt instead.

“Breakfast first,” I tell the cat. “Virtue’s easier on a full stomach.”

I dress, gather my gear, and head downstairs with the cat, keeping clear of the yard’s game.

I give Hedda three silver. “Breakfast paid, then. What’s the room for another night? I’d rather not promise you an empty bed.”

I glance toward the two merchants. “And who’s hiring for the Nashkel road? That gentleman sounds as though he knows more than the notice says.”

I carry my plate over to the window table.

“James Worgen. Soldier once, hired blade since. May I sit?”

I nod toward Lusk. “I heard you say the wagons weren’t robbed. What’s been found—or who’s come back—to tell the difference?”

“Possibly. But a lot of boots have already swallowed four wagons. Three blades might not settle it.”

I set down my fork. “I’ve done scouting, and I can work magic. Before I agree: what’s the pay, who else have you hired, and how many people vanished with those wagons?”

“And can I find Freely here today? I’d rather hear what he saw before we put your last wagon on that road.”

“Eleven people deserves a look. I’ll speak to Freely and give you my answer this afternoon. Don’t count me hired yet.”

I finish my breakfast, then head south with Penny, following the stream past the last forge and listening for Freely’s axe.

“Lusk told me where to find you. James Worgen.”

I stay on my side of the stream. “He’s asked me to guard his last wagon tomorrow. Before I agree, I’d like to know what I’d be walking into. I’m not asking you to go back.”

“He told me about the ruts heading east, and the boots. What else did you notice out there that made you decide to turn round?”

“Not on the strength of three hired swords, no. I’ve seen marching columns take carts before. I’d want to know where this one goes before offering it another.”

I nod toward him. “You’ve given me more to work with than the notice did. Thank you.”

My eyes briefly follow the movement of his hand, then return to his face. “Did you find something out on the rocks? If there’s another warning to be had, I’d sooner hear it here.”

“James Worgen. Soldier once, hired blade since. May I sit?”

I nod toward Lusk. “I heard you say the wagons weren’t robbed. What’s been found—or who’s come back—to tell the difference?”
turns.reply:
Penny gets down from her place by the hearth and follows the plate across the room. She stays a pace behind James's boots, as if the bacon were still on it.

Dalmer looks up from his bread, looks at the plate, and pushes the salt cellar aside with one thick finger to make room. Lusk half rises, then sits again. He can't decide which would be more polite.

"Sit, please. Sit. Lusk. Hal Lusk. Cloth and salt, Beregost to Nashkel, ore and hides back." He talks fast, as if each sentence costs him something. "Nobody's come back, Master Worgen. That's the first thing. Not a driver, not an ox, not a wheel."

He leans in over the table.

"I've been robbed twice in twenty years. I know what it looks like. You find the wagon burnt in a ditch and the oxen butchered for meat. Somebody's always alive with his head broken, and he tells you how many there were. This time there's nothing. And the goods..." He taps the table. "Every bale I send has my mark on it, a blue L stitched in the corner. Bandits sell what they take, and they sell it close, because they can't carry it far. I've had men asking in Nashkel, here, at the Friendly Arm. Not one yard of my cloth has turned up. Nobody's salt has turned up. Four wagons, and nothing for sale anywhere."

"Tell him about Freely," Dalmer says, without looking up.

"I'm getting there." Lusk ticks the points off on his fingers. "The last one was Pell's wagon, eleven days ago. I paid a woodsman two gold to go and look, Tam Freely, he cuts timber south of town. About half a day past where the Fist riders turn round, he found where the ruts leave the road. They go east into the scrub, towards the hills. He followed them maybe a mile, to stony ground, and he lost them there. He wouldn't go any further. Said he'd been paid to look, not to follow."

Dalmer finally sets his bread down. "I drank with Freely after. He said there were no horses. Just the oxen, the wheels, and boots on both sides of the wagon. A lot of boots." He shrugs. "Make of it what you like."

James knows this part from his own years with the scouts, not from anyone's story. Iron tyres scrape stone. A loaded wagon leaves a trail across rocky ground too, if the man following knows to look for bright scratches instead of ruts. And men who take a wagon whole and drive it off the road on foot aren't after what's in it. In Tethyr he saw the free companies do the same thing to farmers' carts. They took the wagon, the beasts and the man holding the reins, because they had a baggage train to fill and somewhere to take it. That wasn't robbery. It was requisition.

Under the table, Penny has settled where she can watch Dalmer's boots and the door at once.

Lusk sees James's face and misreads it, or reads it right. He wets his lips. His eyes go to the old regimental cloak and stay on it.

"I've one wagon left. I'm sending it tomorrow at first light, because if I don't, I've nothing to sell in Nashkel this season, and then..." He stops before the sentence gets to money. "I need two blades. Three, if I can get them. A soldier and a scout... Are you looking for work, Master Worgen?"

turns.message:
“Possibly. But a lot of boots have already swallowed four wagons. Three blades might not settle it.”

I set down my fork. “I’ve done scouting, and I can work magic. Before I agree: what’s the pay, who else have you hired, and how many people vanished with those wagons?”

“And can I find Freely here today? I’d rather hear what he saw before we put your last wagon on that road.”
turns.reply:
Lusk looks at the fork, then at James. Something in his face eases a little, the way it does when a man hears his own fears said aloud by someone who isn't frightened of them.

"Magic," he says. He glances at Dalmer, who has stopped chewing. "Well. Well, that's... I won't say no to that."

He takes the questions in order, fast, like a man reading out a bill.

"Pay. Ten gold a head to Nashkel. Five now, five when the wagon's in the yard at Nashkel. Your board on the road is mine, and your bed in Nashkel the first night." He stops, wets his lips, and goes on before anyone can answer. "It's three days if the weather holds. That's better than the Fist pays a man for a month."

The figure comes out smoothly, too smoothly, like something he's said to himself in the dark a few times. The notice by the door said GOOD PAY. Ten gold is fair pay, not good pay.

"Who else. Nobody yet." He doesn't dress it up. "One fellow came by last night and read the paper. He asked where the wagons went missing and walked out. I'm driving it myself, if it comes to that. I've no drivers left to send."

Then his hands come up onto the table, and he counts without seeming to notice he's doing it.

"How many. First wagon, before Greengrass: Old Corran and his boy. Second: Wil Hask driving, two guards. Third: Bettany Marsh driving, two guards. Brothers, the guards were, from Nashkel. Fourth, Pell, with one guard. I couldn't afford two by then." His fingers stop. "Eleven. Eleven people. And Corran's boy was fourteen."

Dalmer sets down what's left of his bread. "Corran's wife comes here Tenday evenings to ask if there's word," he says to James, flatly. "In case you meet her."

Lusk stares at the table for a moment before going on.

"Freely. He's not here. Days he's at his cut south of town, down along the stream past the last forge. Follow the sound of the axe. Evenings he drinks at the Burning Wizard, across the square." He looks up. "I'll tell you now, he won't thank you for asking. He didn't like what he saw out there, and he liked it less once he'd been paid for it."

Dalmer grunts. "He'll talk to you. He won't go back."

Under the table, Penny has moved. She now sits by James's boot with her back to the room, so she can see Lusk's hands.

Lusk sees James's face and makes himself go on.

"You'd want to see him before you'd say yes. I understand that. I'd do the same." His voice drops. "But the wagon goes at first light, Master Worgen, with you or without you. I need to know by this afternoon, so I can find someone else if it's no."

turns.message:
“Eleven people deserves a look. I’ll speak to Freely and give you my answer this afternoon. Don’t count me hired yet.”

I finish my breakfast, then head south with Penny, following the stream past the last forge and listening for Freely’s axe.
turns.reply:
Lusk nods too quickly, the way a man does when he has decided to hear "not yet" as better than "no."

"This afternoon. Yes. That's fair." He reaches for his cup, finds it empty and puts it down again. "Tell Freely I sent you. Or don't. He might talk more if you don't."

Dalmer says nothing. He pushes the last of the bread toward Penny, who looks at it and then at him, and does not take it.

You finish the eggs. The bacon has gone where bacon goes. Hedda is busy at the counter as you pass, and the board by the door gives you the small print on Lusk's notice at last: *Apply Hal Lusk, Lantern and Tongs. Wagon departs first light, 3rd inst.* Nothing more than that.

Outside, Beregost has fully woken. The main street is a long run of open forge doors, and each one breathes heat as you pass. A boy is leading two oxen to be shod. A Lathanderite acolyte in rose-coloured wool is chalking the price of candles on the temple wall. South of the square the houses thin out and the forges get rougher: lean-tos with stone hearths and slag heaps behind them. The last one is a dwarf-built shed with a black chimney. Past it the road drops to a stream, brown with run-off at the edges and clear in the middle, and a footpath follows it south into alder and ash.

The hammers fade behind you. Inside a quarter of an hour the loudest things are the water and Penny, who has decided the path is hers. She walks a few yards ahead with her tail up and stops now and then to look into the reeds as if they owed her money.

Then you hear the axe. The strokes come steady and unhurried, the sound of a man who swings for a living and doesn't waste any.

The cut is a clearing on the far bank, where the stream widens enough to wade. Trunks are stacked and barked along one side. A mule stands hobbled in the shade, and a two-wheeled timber cart has one shaft propped on a stump. In the middle of it all a man in his fifties is working an ash tree that is nearly down. He's wiry, grey-stubbled, and has his shirt off despite the morning chill. He sees you before you reach the water. The axe stops at the top of its swing, comes down slowly, and stays in his hand.

Penny halts on the near bank and sits. The mule's ears go flat at her.

The woodsman looks at the rapier, at the cloak, at the cat. When he speaks it's across the stream, flat, without raising his voice much.

"If Lusk sent you, I've had my two gold and I've told him what I saw. If he didn't, this is private timber." He shifts his grip on the haft. "Which is it?"

turns.message:
“Lusk told me where to find you. James Worgen.”

I stay on my side of the stream. “He’s asked me to guard his last wagon tomorrow. Before I agree, I’d like to know what I’d be walking into. I’m not asking you to go back.”

“He told me about the ruts heading east, and the boots. What else did you notice out there that made you decide to turn round?”
turns.reply:
Freely hears the name and lets out a short breath through his nose. It isn't quite a laugh. He doesn't put the axe down, but he lets the head rest on the ground and leans on the haft.

"Honest, anyway." He looks at you across the water for a while, then at Penny, who has started watching the mule. The mule watches her back. "Not asking me to go back. Good. I wouldn't."

He's quiet long enough that you start to think that's all you'll get. Then he jerks his chin south, toward the road.

"Past where the Fist riders turn round there's a dead oak, split by lightning, on the left side going south. Two hundred paces after that, east side. That's where it left the road. You'd not see it from the wagon seat. Somebody cut broom and swept the verge behind them, the first fifty feet or so. I only found it because they threw the broom in the ditch and it was wilting."

He shifts his grip on the haft.

"The boots. Dalmer told you a lot of boots. It's more than that. Nailed soles, same nails, same pattern, near enough every one. Two files of them, one each side of the wagon, keeping pace with the oxen. Nobody straggling and nobody stepping off to piss. I've tracked deer, and I've tracked lads poaching deer. Poachers wander. These didn't." He counts it in his head without moving his lips. "Ten. Twelve, maybe. Hard to tell, they walked in each other's prints."

You heard enough of this in Tethyr to fill in what he's left out. He's describing hobnailed marching boots, a column, and men on march discipline with a cart in the middle. It's the same picture you got at breakfast, and now somebody's actually seen it.

"Stony ground's about a mile in. Scrub gives out, it's all shelf rock and gravel, slopes up toward the hills. Trail stops there like a cut rope." He looks down at the axe head. "I stood there a while."

His thumb goes to the small leather pouch tied at his belt, rests on it for a moment, and comes away again. He doesn't look at it. He doesn't look at you either.

"Twelve men who march in step and sweep up after themselves don't want finding. Anyone who finds them ends up counted with the rest. That's why I turned round." He lifts the axe off the ground, not into a swing, just back into his hands. "That's what Lusk's two gold bought him. You can have it for nothing."

Then, flatly, his eyes back on you:

"You taking his wagon down there?"

turns.message:
“Not on the strength of three hired swords, no. I’ve seen marching columns take carts before. I’d want to know where this one goes before offering it another.”

I nod toward him. “You’ve given me more to work with than the notice did. Thank you.”

My eyes briefly follow the movement of his hand, then return to his face. “Did you find something out on the rocks? If there’s another warning to be had, I’d sooner hear it here.”
turns.reply:
Freely watches your eyes go to his belt and come back to his face. He doesn't hide the pouch, and he doesn't touch it again. The axe stays where it is, head down in the wood chips. On the near bank Penny has turned her torn ear toward him and gone still.

For a while the only sounds are the stream and the mule shifting its weight.

He gets there first, and it isn't the answer you asked for.

"I found rock." He says it flatly, and he holds your eye while he says it. "Gravel, and rock, and nobody's tracks after that. I told Lusk and I've told you." He takes the axe up out of the chips and sets his feet. "You've had your warning. Don't go where they went."

You know what a man looks like when he has shut a door, and Freely has shut this one. The thanks landed, and so did your honesty about the wagon. Whatever is in that pouch isn't going to cross the stream on the strength of one conversation with a stranger who carries a sword.

He turns back to the ash. The first stroke goes in clean and hard, then a second. Between the third and the fourth he speaks again without looking round. His voice doesn't rise; it doesn't have to.

"Lusk'll drive it himself if nobody goes. He's that kind of fool." The axe bites. "Corran's boy used to bring my bread out here, Tendays."

After that there's only the axe. The tree creaks and starts to lean.

Penny gets up from the bank and gives the woodsman a long, level look. Then she walks back along the path toward town, tail up, as if the meeting were over and she had been the one to end it.

---

opening.text:
Morning comes to Beregost the way it always does here: first the bells of Lathander's temple, then the hammers. By the time the light slips through the shutters, half the town's forges are already ringing.

The room above the Lantern and Tongs is small and honest — a bed, a washstand, your gear where you left it, and the heavy purse that still feels like it belongs to someone luckier. Three hundred and fifty gold, give or take. No debt to collect, no caravan to guard, no one waiting for you anywhere today.

The cat is not on the bed. It sits by the door, tail curled around its paws, watching the gap under the frame with steady attention. A moment later you hear why, or part of why: heavy, unhurried steps on the stairs, and a woman's voice through the wood.

"Morning up there! Porridge and bacon's on, eggs if you're quick. Will you be wanting it brought up, or are you coming down?"

From the yard beneath the window drifts another sound — the clatter of a barrel being rolled into place, the slap of a deck being squared, and a carter calling out that there's room for one more if anyone's feeling lucky before the smith gets to their wheels.

The steps stop outside your door. The cat looks up at you.

epilogue.text:
Epilogue — the table closed on 25 October 2026 after 7 turns

Noon came to the Lantern and Tongs, and no one told Hedda Brask about the room. She stripped the bed and let it to a wool factor from Baldur's Gate before the bells had finished. The breakfast was long since paid, three silver taken from a gold piece, seven counted back. Her ledger has no line against the name Worgen, and she has never had cause to remember it.

Hal Lusk waited at the window table all afternoon with an empty cup. Nobody came. At first light on the third he drove his last wagon south himself. Dalmer sat on the seat beside him and grumbled about fools the whole way. They passed the split oak at a trot and did not look east. Nothing came out of the scrub. Three days later they rolled into Nashkel, sold the cloth and salt, and Lusk sold the wagon and oxen too. He spends the winter clerking for a chandler in Beregost. He does not talk about the road, and he no longer counts on his fingers.

Two weeks after the wagon left, a Flaming Fist captain rode in from Nashkel with thirty riders. Tam Freely met her in the Burning Wizard one evening and set a small leather pouch on the table. What was in it never became common talk, but she bought him a drink and he took the Fist east past the shelf rock. Three days into the hills they found a camp. It had been struck clean. There were fire pits filled in, a corral of cut stakes, and the burnt iron of four wagon tyres in a heap. A grave lay under the cairn at the far end. The Fist did not open it. The column was gone, and no wagon has gone missing on the Nashkel road since the first frost. The captain wrote her report, the riders came home, and the matter was closed.

None of the eleven came back: not Old Corran or his boy, not Wil Hask or Bettany Marsh, not the brothers from Nashkel, not Pell or the guard he could afford. Corran's wife still comes to the Lantern and Tongs on Tenday evenings. Hedda gives her a cup of something hot and says there is no word. In time the visits have become a habit more than a question.

Freely still works his cut below the last forge. In the cold months the stream runs clear all the way across. Somebody else brings him his bread now, and he pays them a copper extra. He has not been south of the oak again.

The dwarf in the scorched apron eats his porridge at the same table with his back to the wall. Orrin Tabb still deals at the barrelhead in the yard. He calls for one sporting soul, and now and then he gets one.

The place where Pell's wagon left the road has grown over. Broom has come back along the verge, and the ruts have filled with leaf and rain. A carter who did not know to look would see only scrub.

Beregost goes on as Beregost does: the bells of Lathander first, then the hammers.

Some of the regulars half remember a man in a Tethyrian cloak who carried his plate across the room to sit with strangers. They recall a grey cat with a torn ear, which walked a few paces ahead of him down the stream path, as though it had decided the way. He was there one morning and asked good questions. Then he was gone, and the town did not wonder long where.
